newsitem.title: QATAR: Owner nations asked to help indebted Gulf Air.
newsitem.headline: Owner nations asked to help indebted Gulf Air.

text.p: Gulf Air shareholders on Thursday brushed aside plans by Abu Dhabi to increase its holding in the indebted regional carrier but asked partners to extend loans to ease the cash crisis.

"The extraordinary board meeting deferred the proposal to increase the airline's capital but allowed shareholders to give it loans to meet the situation", said Qatar's Minister of Transport and Communications, Ahmed bin Nasser al-Thani.

The amount of the loan, to be offered by each of the four governments who equally own the airline -- Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain and Abu Dhabi -- has been left to their "sweet will", he told reporters at the end of the two-day meeting in Doha.
Abu Dhabi had offered to pump in fresh capital and loans to help the airline, facing $2 billion in debt, in return for an increase in its shareholding, officials said.
But Qatar and Oman opposed the offer, fearing the move would allow Abu Dhabi to take control of the Manama-based carrier.
"The board decision does not alter the balance of shareholding," Sheikh Ahmed said.
"The board has decided to conduct more studies and collect more information on the issue of raising the capital", he said.
Gulf Air's present difficulties mainly stem from a lavish buying of costly aircrafts on loans and opening numerous uneconomic routes in the 1980s.
"The agreement is really a milestone and it will help Gulf Air to continue flying and provide service to this area," Sheikh Ahmed said.
"We believe the company is doing a very important service for the region and it is in the best interest of everybody to ensure that Gulf Air is flying."
In 1995, the company closed its books with $159 million in net losses and was unable to service its loans.
"This year our top priority will be to cut down on operations and increase profits", said Gulf Air chief Sheikh Ahmed bin Seif al-Nahyan.
The airline, which has 32 aircraft, has leased some of its fleet to other airlines to raise income and closed some of its uneconomic routes.
